Header: 2026-03-05 15:00 PDT | Duration: 48 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samantha (Redwood AE), Rahul (Redwood SE), Jamie (CSM), Marcus (CISO, StellarBank), Priya (SRE), Elena (Legal), Tom (Infra), Ava (Compliance)

Redwood ran tabletop scenarios around an outage and a KMS compromise. Customer asked about RTO/RPO guarantees, audit log retention, and SSO/RBAC mapping. Action: Redwood to share SLA draft, SE to share KMS checklist, schedule a resilience window.

[00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, appreciate it. Quick roll call — can you confirm who we have?
[00:05] Marcus: Marcus here — CISO.
[00:07] Priya: Priya, SRE.
[00:09] Elena: Elena from legal.
[00:10] Tom: Tom, infra.
[00:12] Ava: Ava, compliance.
[00:14] Samantha: Great. Rahul and I from Redwood. Jamie's on the call too. The plan for today is a tabletop — focus on incident response, BCDR objectives RTO/RPO, SLOs and SLA wording, and the escalation path. We'll walk through three scenarios, stop for questions. Sound good?
[00:28] Marcus: Sounds good. Our priority is ledger availability and data integrity; other features are secondary.
[00:33] Rahul: Noted. For context, Redwood's private deployment option allows you to run a control plane in your VPC, or an on-prem package if you need air-gapped. We do KMS integration via customer-managed keys — support for AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and a set of HSM vendors.
[00:50] Priya: Can you spell out how you handle key rotation and any live rekey? We need guarantees around keys not causing a mass outage during rotation.
[00:58] Rahul: Yeah, so in our standard flow, keys are used to encrypt disk and secrets; we support envelope encryption. Rotation is staged: new keys written and services pick them up with a rolling restart. For private on-prem deployments we have a hot-swap process and a brief cache invalidation window — typically under 5 minutes for token caches but ledger re-encryption is async, so we wouldn't re-encrypt buckets in-line.
[01:20] Elena: Does that require us to accept any downtime? Our compliance folks want clear RTO/RPO numbers tied to encryption events.
[01:27] Samantha: Great question. Let's use concrete targets — Marcus, what are your target RTO and RPO for the ledger itself versus metadata?
[01:33] Marcus: For the core ledger we want RTO <= 1 hour, RPO <= 15 minutes. For metadata/search/indexing, RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour.
[01:44] Samantha: Ok. Internally Redwood's default for hosted is generally RTO in tens of minutes for a single-region failure with fallback, but since this is a private deployment we should map the SLAs explicitly. Rahul, is 1 hour RTO for ledger feasible with our private setup?
[01:58] Rahul: Yes, with dedicated capacity and warm standby we can hit 1 hour. Key caveat is the replication method — if you're doing cross-region async replication, recoverability depends on last replicated sequence. That's where RPO comes in; to hit 15 minutes you need frequent checkpoints. We can configure continuous WAL shipping or periodic snapshots.
[02:18] Priya: WAL shipping adds network egress — can you quantify cost and overhead?
[02:22] Rahul: There's some overhead; depends on throughput. We estimate X GB per million requests, but we'll provide a tailored calc.
[02:29] Tom: On the network side, our firewall policies restrict outbound connections to specific Redwood endpoints — do you have a documented list of IPs and ports?
[02:36] Samantha: Yes, we'll include an endpoint allowlist and an ops playbook. Also note for private air-gapped installs we can do a bundle install, but that changes upgrade ops.
[02:46] Ava: Audit logging question — how long are logs retained and do they contain key usage events?
[02:50] Rahul: Audit logs for control plane actions are kept for 90 days by default in the console; for private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM — we support structured JSON with syscall-style events, including key unwrap/usage events. If you need longer retention we can configure S3 export to your retention bucket.
[03:08] Marcus: Important: any audit events that reveal key material or unencrypted secrets must never be in logs.
[03:13] Rahul: Totally, we never log secret material; we only log key IDs and envelope operations.
[03:18] Samantha: Okay let's move to scenario one: region outage. We'll simulate a primary region experiencing total network loss.
[03:25] [Scenario 1 start]
[03:26] Samantha: In this event, traffic should failover to warm standby in secondary region. Who's oncall at Stellar? Priya?
[03:31] Priya: Yes, our oncall rotates weekly — me this week. We need to understand the escalation path — Redwood's first, second, third lines?
[03:38] Rahul: Our standard escalation for private customers is: first-level Redwood infra on-call (30 min ack), then SE escalation to on-shift SRE (1 hr), then product ops lead (2 hours). We can customize overlap windows — e.g., 24/7 pager for critical incidents. We also support webhook/PagerDuty integration.
[03:55] Tom: Are we able to configure on-call overlaps? We want a Redwood primary contact and a secondary on our side to be paged simultaneously.
[04:02] Samantha: Absolutely, we can set dual escalation paths. We'll include sample PagerDuty playbook in the runbook.
[04:07] Marcus: SLA credits—what's the SLA for multi-region failover? We see 99.95% cited in docs; we want to see how credits are computed.
[04:16] Samantha: We'll pull up the SLA language later, but yes 99.95% is our higher tier for dedicated deployments; we can show the credit table. There's also a failure-modes appendix that clarifies planned maintenance exclusions.
[04:28] Elena: Please ensure maintenance windows are mutually agreed and we have a 72-hour notice for disruptive ops.
[04:34] Samantha: Noted.
[04:36] [00:04:36 approx — brief crosstalk while screen is shared]
[04:55] Rahul: For the failover, we rely on DNS failover plus active health checks and a routing layer. For private VPC, failover can be via load balancer switch or BGP if you prefer. BGP gives faster cutover but requires network changes on your side.
[05:12] Priya: BGP is heavy; we prefer DNS TTL-based failover, but TTL can be slow for some clients. What's your typical cutover time with DNS?
[05:20] Rahul: With low TTL and pre-warmed endpoints, we've seen median cutover around 90-180 seconds for traffic, but for sessionful workloads there is some reconnect logic.
[05:30] Marcus: That 2–3 minutes is fine, as long as we can meet the RTO objective of under an hour for ledger recovery.
[05:36] [Scenario 1 end — notes captured]
[05:38] Samantha: Scenario two — data corruption / accidental deletion of a bucket or object. How do you detect and recover?
[05:45] Rahul: We recommend multi-tier backups — S3-style immutable snapshots, a replication scheme, and point-in-time restore. For ledger data we support WAL + snapshot restore. Recovery time depends on data size and restore bandwidth. For small to medium workloads we can expect under 1 hour if snapshotting and transfer links are healthy.
[06:02] Tom: I want to note that our on-prem bandwidth to offsite backups is limited overnight — that will affect restores.
[06:07] Samantha: Okay, so we'll flag that in the runbook as a constraint and include a prioritized restore plan (critical tables, then indexes).
[06:14] Marcus: RPO for deletion events — does Redwood support point-in-time recovery to a specific sequence number?
[06:19] Rahul: Yes, with WAL we can replay to a sequence or timestamp, assuming the WALs were persisted. If your WALs are shipped every 5 minutes you get RPO=5 minutes, logically.
[06:27] Priya: We need to validate WAL retention windows and ensure they aren't pruned too aggressively.
[06:32] Rahul: We'll include recommended retention parameters.
[06:34] [Scenario 2 end]
[06:36] Samantha: Scenario three — suspected KMS compromise. This is a big one so stay with me. Internal detection shows unauthorized key unwrap attempts.
[06:45] Marcus: First, we rotate keys, revoke the compromised key, and validate data decryptability. But we need to be clear: if a key is compromised and it's used for envelope encryption of many objects, re-encrypting in-line could be huge. What's Redwood's stepwise recommendation?
[06:59] Rahul: Step 1: isolate key usage and revoke. Step 2: failover to secondary key while ensuring service continuity via envelope decryption with the revoked key only for reads if allowed. Step 3: schedule re-encryption of newly written objects with new key. Full bulk re-encrypt is scheduled and throttled. The immediate goal is to prevent further usage and maintain reads where possible.
[07:18] Ava: We need to ensure any legal hold or retention requirements are preserved; can't destroy data while an investigation is ongoing.
[07:23] Elena: Also want to understand notification obligations under our contract and regulator — e.g., notify affected parties within X days.
[07:29] Samantha: We'll surface the notification language in the SLA draft. For PII exposures there are reporting obligations; we'll flag contract escape clauses.
[07:36] Marcus: On the runbook side, who declares a security incident? Who escalates externally?
[07:40] Rahul: Usually a joint declaration — customer ops or security declares; Redwood's SE/incident commander supports. For public-facing incidents Redwood coordinates messaging only with your approval.
[07:50] Priya: Do you have a tabletop or simulated compromise runbook we can run with our team?
[07:54] Jamie: Yes — we have a resilience test kit (doc + checklist + sample PD playbook). We'll include that and propose a joint drill.
[08:02] Samantha: Ok near the end — let's recap next steps. Marcus, you mentioned RTO/RPO; you'll share current spreadsheets. Rahul will send KMS checklist. I'll send the SLA draft and a sample escalation runbook. We'll align on a resilience test week of 2026-03-23.
[08:17] Marcus: Sounds good. Couple of small clarifying points — can you add a line item for audit log integrity checks? We want tamper-evidence and chain-of-custody for logs.
[08:27] Rahul: We support signed log export and can add hash chaining to the export process; we will provide examples.
[08:34] Tom: Also want a table of potential latencies during failover vs normal ops. Can you include typical token latency and worst-case tails?
[08:41] Samantha: Absolutely. We'll send performance tail-percentile numbers and token-cost tradeoffs in follow-up.
[08:47] Elena: From legal perspective, please also include sample indemnity language around data breaches in the SLA packet.
[08:53] Samantha: We'll include a negotiable section for legal review.
[08:56] [Final minutes — informal wrap-up]
[09:01] Marcus: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the SLA and the KMS doc, and the proposed dates.
[09:05] Samantha: Thanks — we'll get those over quickly. One housekeeping note: if anyone sees transcripts have mistakes, flag them and we'll correct.
[09:10] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[09:12] (call end)
